entities.rationale: Poor, aid-dependent island state with weak government, high undernourishment and low safe-water access; food imports and governance are the weak points, while political calm helps.
Stable high-island state exposed to cyclones and coastal flooding; remittances and aid keep the basics going, but low income makes near-free essentials unlikely without superintelligence.
Upper-middle-income tourism economy; hurricanes, high public debt and rising violent crime are the main threats, but recovery capacity is decent.
Low-lying atolls facing sea-level rise, wave flooding and salinised freshwater lenses; loss of water and habitable land dominates, and emigration routes are limited.
Relatively rich and well governed with granite high islands; coastal erosion and dependence on imported food and fuel are the main exposures.
Stable small state with good adaptation readiness; major hurricanes like Ivan and Beryl are the recurring shock, but recovery has taken months to a few years, not a lasting loss.
Highest climate vulnerability in this group, with many outer atolls; high islands and US compact funding and migration rights cushion it, but reliance on that funding is a risk.
Rich, mostly outside the hurricane belt and backed by the Netherlands, but it runs on desalinated water and imported food and fuel, and aging raises health costs.
US territory with a federal backstop and high income, but hurricanes like Irma and Maria cut power for months, homicide is very high and the population is aging fast.

Low-lying islands exposed to cyclones, tsunamis and volcanic shocks like the 2022 eruption, with poor safe-water access; diaspora remittances and stability help, but income is too low for near-free essentials without superintelligence.
Debt above 100% of GDP, very high homicide, hurricanes and the La Soufriere volcano are the main risks; it remains a stable democracy with full electricity access.
Fairly rich tourism economy; low-lying Barbuda, which was evacuated after Irma, and water scarcity met by desalination are the main exposures.
Rich, well governed and embedded between France and Spain, so collapse is mostly the global risk; getting essentials under 10% of income needs superintelligence-driven cost drops.
Mountainous island repeatedly hit by hurricanes, with Maria destroying much of its housing, and debt near 100% of GDP; strong adaptation readiness helps it recover.
Relatively rich with solid governance, but the highest homicide rate in this group and hurricane exposure are the main risks.
Very rich, almost debt-free and well governed inside the Swiss system, so collapse is nearly all global risk; very high income per resident already puts essentials close to the 10% line.
Extremely high income and protection by France make local collapse unlikely; the very old population pushes health costs up, which keeps essentials near rather than clearly below 10% of income.
Atolls about two meters above sea level face flooding and loss of freshwater; US compact funding and migration rights are the main buffer, though many residents may leave.
Rich hilltop enclave inside Italy, so its fate tracks Italy and the world; high water stress is covered by Italian supply.
Middle-income with US compact backing and a large volcanic main island, but typhoons, low outer islands and reef-dependent food and tourism are exposed; tension around Taiwan adds security risk.
